name: Yusuf Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m from the independent Work Futures Panel. We are separate from employers, unions, AI companies and government, and this is confidential. What is your working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Yusuf Schmidt, 58, with a vocational certificate and a junior lineworker’s place at the electricity company. I was a delivery driver before this, so I know the roads but I am still learning how to build and repair overhead lines. We meet at the yard, inspect the lifting gear, then work through outages or new connections. I like finding the one failed joint that darkened a block. I am careful on the pole because my hands have not yet learned every movement.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who shares the consequences of a long or short week with you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Amira is a home-care aide, and our grown daughter lives in another town. We have about two and a half months of expenses saved and a mortgage that keeps me looking at the pay calendar. I use an AI app now and then to explain an unfamiliar diagram, after another worker has shown me the right source. I will try a tool that has proved useful, but I will not let a screen sign off a live line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that a little quicker filing does not change our job at the pole. I would like the office to send clearer work packets, though. A missing address costs us a drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the line work and my ordinary pay to hold in this picture. The mortgage still makes me attentive to Amira’s care shifts, which can drop if a client leaves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the morning lifting-gear check and take my assigned repairs. Starting this month I’d put fifty from each pay against the mortgage principal; in 2029 I’d keep that up if both our hours stayed normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the technology in this version, though not careless about money. A quiet year would give us a chance to reduce what we owe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would clearer paperwork fix?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last Tuesday the packet had a house number but no street, and we drove back to the yard for the right address. I would ask the office for one clean address field before buying any new system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Amira has fewer shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Amira and I keep separate notes on our hours, then compare them on Sunday. If her care rota thins, I would stop the extra mortgage payment until the bills were covered.

say: I’d tell coworkers **line repair** stays much the same.
I’d ask the office for **complete addresses** in each work packet.
think: I expect my **ordinary wages** to hold in this picture.
Our **mortgage** still depends partly on Amira’s changing care shifts.
do: Keep **assigned repairs** and the morning lifting-gear checks.
Pay **fifty extra** toward the mortgage when both work schedules hold.
feel: I feel **calm about AI** and attentive to household pay.
S0.quote: A missing address costs us a drive.
fieldNote: Yusuf focuses on the **work packet** because his delivery background makes wasted travel especially visible.
His mortgage payment plan is expressly **conditional on two incomes**, showing caution beneath his relaxed public line.

steps.text: Take assigned repairs and inspect lifting gear each morning
Pay fifty extra toward mortgage principal while both schedules hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that smarter scheduling could save driving time if the addresses and isolation notes are right. I would want the dispatch workers and lineworkers to test the new route before it becomes a target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the office might need fewer people to write packets, and our crew could face more calls per day. I am junior and still learning, so if the company measures only speed I could lose shifts even while the wires need hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d ask the supervisor to let our crew compare one month of software routes with actual travel and repair times. In 2029 I’d keep taking shifts, use the AI app to explain the new packet codes after a colleague checks them, and take our findings to the staff meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel hopeful about less driving and nervous about being timed. I have seen a route look perfect on a map and fail at the locked gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which route would a system miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One substation gate is on the service road, not the public street. If dispatch sends a truck to the street side, the time loss is real even if the software calls it our delay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you raise the timing issue?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the staff meeting the log, not accuse dispatch of being lazy. They need a way to correct bad addresses, and we need a fair allowance for testing.

say: I’d support **tested scheduling** that saves travel without cutting electrical checks.
I’d ask **dispatch and line crews** to examine routes together.
think: I fear **speed targets** could reduce my junior shifts.
Office packet roles may shrink before physical **line repair** does.
do: Compare **software routes** with a month of actual travel and repair times.
Keep **paid shifts** in 2029 and use AI to explain checked packet codes.
Bring the **route log** to a staff meeting.
feel: I feel **hopeful about travel**, nervous about timing targets.
S1.quote: I have seen a route look perfect on a map and fail at the locked gate.
fieldNote: Yusuf’s former delivery work gives him a **route test** grounded in gates and actual travel time.
He is willing to use AI for packet codes after **colleague checks**, but fears speed-only measures of a junior worker.

steps.text: Take paid line shifts while the crew tests new routes
Use AI to explain packet codes after a colleague verifies them
Bring a month of route and repair times to the staff meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full thinking AI by 2028 may write the outage plans, while the crew still climbs until capable robots arrive around 2031. I would ask the company to show which paid jobs are open before it tells us to retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 60 when planning changes and 63 when the physical repair could be done by a robot. Two and a half months saved would not carry our mortgage if I lost my line wage, and Amira’s care income is not enough alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d ask for a written mortgage balance and stop the extra principal payments so cash can build. In 2029 I’d keep line shifts and apply for the utility’s depot driver job if posted; before 2031 I’d ask the training office whether a paid equipment course actually leads to a vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about losing the wage, even with a possible driving fallback. The old delivery work helps me apply; it does not make the company keep a driver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could depot driving last after robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a line robot needed deliveries, a depot driver might still be useful for a while. If robots also move equipment, that job could go too, so I would ask about the contract term before leaving the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes at home first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Amira and I would pause the bathroom renovation we have priced out. Our grown daughter has her own bills, and I would not ask her to cover a mortgage we chose.

say: I’d ask for **real paid vacancies** before any retraining promise.
I’d distinguish **2028 planning AI** from capable line robots around 2031.
think: At **63**, I could lose line pay while we still owe a mortgage.
Our **small reserve** and Amira’s care wage cannot replace my income.
do: Stop **extra mortgage payments** and check the balance this month.
Keep **line shifts** in 2029 and apply for depot driving if posted.
Ask about a **paid equipment course** only if tied to a vacancy.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about the wage, despite a possible driving fallback.
S2.quote: The old delivery work helps me apply; it does not make the company keep a driver.
fieldNote: Yusuf turns first to the **mortgage balance**, shifting from extra principal payments to available cash.
His depot driving idea uses prior experience, while he recognizes **robot logistics** could make that role temporary.

steps.text: Check the mortgage balance and pause extra principal payments
Keep paid line repair shifts through 2029
Apply for a posted utility depot driver opening

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell coworkers that five years allows the company to publish a proper staffing plan instead of sending us rumours. Thinking AI could take outage planning in 2031, and capable line robots could arrive around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 at the first date and 66 at the second. I might be able to stop climbing by then, but I do not know our pension figures or how much mortgage will remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d get a pension estimate and work out a mortgage payoff schedule with Amira. In 2032 I’d keep line shifts and apply for the depot driver opening if one appeared; before 2034 I’d ask the company to train me on equipment logistics if there were paid posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy, with enough time to make a real budget. The danger is making a five-year plan out of a job advertisement that never appears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make logistics credible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a logistics post existed, I could bring my delivery experience and learn the utility’s stock controls. I would not enroll in a course before asking whether there is a paid place at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the mortgage be gone by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our mortgage has six years left on the current schedule. Extra payments might shorten it if shifts stay steady, but I would not use the emergency reserve to make a neat date.

say: I’d ask for a **published staffing plan** during the five-year warning.
I’d separate **2031 outage planning** from capable robots around 2034.
think: I might stop climbing at **66**, but pension and mortgage figures remain uncertain.
A **depot vacancy** is only a possibility, not a plan by itself.
do: Get a **pension estimate** and write a mortgage schedule with Amira.
Keep **line shifts** in 2032 and apply for a depot opening if posted.
Ask about **paid logistics training** tied to real posts before 2034.
feel: I feel **uneasy but organized**, aware that a vacancy may never appear.
S3.quote: The danger is making a five-year plan out of a job advertisement that never appears.
fieldNote: Yusuf uses the warning years to test **mortgage and pension numbers**, then ties any job move to an actual opening.
His delivery background suggests logistics, but he refuses a course without **paid posts** at the end.

steps.text: Get a pension estimate and draft a mortgage payoff schedule
Keep taking paid line shifts during 2032
Apply for a posted depot driver vacancy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell friends ten years is long enough to check both the work plan and our own budget each year. Thinking AI could handle records in 2036; capable robots could do line repairs around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 when the records change and 71 when robots reach repairs. If we clear the mortgage and get a usable pension, I could be retired first, but I have not seen the pension estimate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d request the estimate and keep the current line job while my shoulders allow. In 2037 I’d take paid equipment deliveries if the utility offered them, and Amira and I would compare pension income with mortgage, care and food costs; if the sums failed, I’d apply for a depot driver post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less pressed with a decade. I still want a route off the pole that depends on an offer and figures, not on wishful thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would equipment deliveries last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can drive the equipment truck and know how to secure a load, but the utility might not need a human driver in 2039. I would take the work if paid now and keep checking what comes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Amira spend on later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Amira wants to visit our daughter more often once we stop full-time work. We will put that travel into the budget only after the mortgage and basic bills are covered.

say: I’d ask for **yearly work plans** through the decade before robots reach repairs.
I’d explain **2036 records** change ahead of hands-on robots around 2039.
think: I could retire before **71** if the mortgage clears and pension income works.
I do not yet have a **pension estimate** to support that choice.
do: Request a **pension estimate** and keep safe line shifts.
Take **paid equipment deliveries** in 2037 if offered.
Apply for a **depot driver post** if retirement income falls short.
feel: I feel **less pressed**, though the route off the pole remains conditional.
S4.quote: I still want a route off the pole that depends on an offer and figures, not on wishful thinking.
fieldNote: Yusuf’s longer outlook rests on **mortgage clearance** and verified pension income rather than an assumed retirement date.
He would take **paid equipment deliveries** while available, even though future robots may remove that work too.

steps.text: Request a pension estimate and compare income with mortgage costs
Keep safe line shifts and take paid equipment deliveries if offered
Apply for a depot driver post if retirement income falls short

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my mortgage would still be there when capable robots reached the line. A list of real paid openings and enough notice to apply would help, along with a training course tied to one of those jobs. I can change direction if I know there is a road to take.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether a late starter feels like a guest on the crew. Sometimes I do. Then I find the right failed joint and the others hand me the tool without making a fuss, and I feel I belong.

headlineQuote: I can change direction if I know there is a road to take.
portrait: Yusuf is a **58-year-old junior lineworker** whose earlier delivery work helps him notice flawed routes and possible depot jobs.
He and partner Amira have **2.5 months** of expenses saved and a mortgage.
He uses **AI occasionally** for unfamiliar diagrams once coworkers have shown him a reliable source.
Across scenarios, he keeps paid shifts, checks **mortgage and pension figures**, and applies for actual depot openings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries Yusuf most because his mortgage could remain when robots reach physical linework.
whatWouldHelp: A **real openings list**, application notice and training tied to paid work would give him a route to change.
